capabilities.label: Primitive
capabilities.means: Key generation, encapsulation or signing, and the matching decapsulation or verification, through the component's own API.
capabilities.default_means: Registered and selectable through the default provider or backend with no build flag or opt-in.

capabilities.label: TLS 1.3
capabilities.means: Use in a TLS 1.3 handshake -- key exchange for a KEM or hybrid group, authentication for a signature scheme.
capabilities.default_means: In the default supported-groups list (key exchange) or the default signature-algorithms list (authentication) as shipped.

capabilities.label: X.509
capabilities.means: Certificates and keys -- generating, parsing, signing, verifying and chain-building with the algorithm; composite and hybrid forms where the algorithm is one.
capabilities.default_means: Accepted in chain verification without an opt-in.

capabilities.label: SSH
capabilities.means: Use in the SSH key exchange or as a host or user key type.
capabilities.default_means: In the default key-exchange or key-type preference list as shipped.

capabilities.label: IPsec / IKEv2
capabilities.means: Use in IKEv2 key exchange or authentication.
capabilities.default_means: In the default IKEv2 proposal as shipped.

capabilities.label: FIPS 140-3
capabilities.means: Standing of the algorithm inside a FIPS 140-3 validated module of the component. See the file header for how the scale reads here.
capabilities.default_means: Inside the validated boundary and enabled in the module's approved mode.

capabilities.label: PKCS#11
capabilities.means: Usable through the PKCS#11 interface -- a mechanism an application can call by name, not merely an algorithm the firmware implements. The distinction is the point of the column: a device can support ML-DSA internally and expose it only through a proprietary SDK, which is a different answer for anyone with existing software. KMIP, JCE and a cloud REST API are adjacent questions and are NOT this column; where they are what a component offers, the cell note says so.
capabilities.default_means: Available through the standard interface as shipped, with no vendor extension or firmware option to enable.

capabilities.label: Firmware signing
capabilities.means: The component's OWN firmware or software updates are signed with the algorithm -- the device's root of trust rather than the keys it holds for you. A module whose customer keys are post-quantum and whose firmware chain is RSA has moved the problem rather than solved it, and this is the column that says so. It is also where stateful hash-based signatures stop being an oddity: firmware signing is the use SP 800-208 exists for.
capabilities.default_means: The shipping firmware chain is signed with it, not an option a customer can enable.

algorithms.label: X-Wing
algorithms.note: A hybrid KEM in the KEM family rather than the hybrid-kex family, and the distinction matters: hybrid-kex rows are NAMED TLS GROUPS negotiated in a handshake, while X-Wing is a KEM construction with its own combiner that an application calls directly. It is NOT X25519MLKEM768 -- same two ingredients, different construction -- and recording one as the other is exactly the mis-file this row was added to fix (2026-09-13). Promoted on the register's own rule that a second component carrying something is the bar: libsodium shipped it in 1.0.22 and Apple's CryptoKit exposes it as XWingMLKEM768X25519.

algorithms.label: X25519MLKEM768
algorithms.note: The hybrid group browsers and CDNs deploy. Pre-standard name X25519Kyber768.

algorithms.label: curveSM2MLKEM768
algorithms.note: Added so a component that ships it (OpenSSL 4.0) can be recorded; expect few cells.

algorithms.label: MLKEM512
algorithms.standard: draft-ietf-tls-mlkem (RFC Editor queue); IANA 0x0200 (512), Recommended N
algorithms.note: Category 1. Few components offer it; most that ship a pure group start at 1024.

algorithms.label: MLKEM768
algorithms.standard: draft-ietf-tls-mlkem (RFC Editor queue); IANA 0x0201 (513), Recommended N

algorithms.label: MLKEM1024
algorithms.standard: draft-ietf-tls-mlkem (RFC Editor queue); IANA 0x0202 (514), Recommended N
algorithms.note: The group a pure-post-quantum mandate asks for (Category 5), and the one most implementations added first (BoringSSL, Go, NSS).

algorithms.label: ML-DSA
algorithms.note: External-mu (pre-hashed mu) signing is recorded in the cell note, not as a row, until two components track it.

algorithms.label: FN-DSA (Falcon)
algorithms.note: Pre-standard Falcon-512/1024 support is recorded here with the note saying so.

algorithms.label: Composite ML-DSA
algorithms.note: ML-DSA paired with an ECDSA, EdDSA or RSA component in one X.509 signature.

why.pure-kex: A pure ML-KEM group has no combiner: the primitive under it is ML-KEM itself, which the ml-kem row's primitive cell already carries. The hybrid rows stay a question here because a hybrid has a combiner of its own to ship or not.

why.composite: The composite drafts register X.509 and CMS algorithm identifiers. TLS has no SignatureScheme codepoint for a composite, so nothing can offer one in a handshake; a composite certificate inside a verified chain is the x509 cell, not this one.
why.stateful-hbs: TLS registers no SignatureScheme for LMS or XMSS, and an online handshake signer -- one key, many signatures, no shared state -- is precisely the use SP 800-208 excludes.

except.why: Since 2026-10-08 pure ML-KEM in a TLS handshake is recorded per NAMED GROUP in the pure-kex rows (MLKEM512, MLKEM768, MLKEM1024), as hybrids are in the hybrid-kex rows. A source that says only "ML-KEM in TLS" without naming a group is a gap on the group rows, not a cell here -- several cells filed here before the split were hybrid evidence of exactly that kind. X-Wing keeps its tls cell as a question: it is not a pure group.

why.hybrid-kex: These rows are named TLS groups: an IANA TLS codepoint negotiated in a handshake, never a certificate key type. A certificate holding an ML-KEM key is the kem row.
why.pure-kex: As for hybrid-kex: these rows are TLS group codepoints. A certificate holding an ML-KEM key is the ml-kem row's x509 cell.
These rows are TLS group codepoints. SSH names its own key exchanges, so any SSH method built on ML-KEM is recorded against the ml-kem row.
why.hybrid-kex: SSH names its own hybrid key exchanges (mlkem768x25519-sha256 and kin) rather than borrowing the TLS groups these rows hold, so an SSH hybrid is recorded against the KEM row it is built from.

why.pure-kex: These rows are TLS group codepoints. IKEv2 negotiates ML-KEM as its own key exchange transform, recorded against the ml-kem row.
why.hybrid-kex: RFC 9370 composes additional key exchanges from single transforms rather than negotiating a TLS group, so an IKEv2 hybrid is recorded against the KEM row it is built from.
why.composite: No IKEv2 implementation or draft defines a composite signature for RFC 7427 authentication. The ASN.1 encoding could in principle carry one, so flip this the day a draft says so.
why.stateful-hbs: IKEv2 registers no LMS or XMSS authentication method.

why.composite: No composite scheme appears in a FIPS standard. CMVP validates the ML-DSA and the ECDSA or RSA component separately, which the signature rows already carry.

except.why: FIPS 206 is still a draft, so there is no standard to validate against and CMVP will not certify a pre-standard scheme. A real question again on the day FIPS 206 is final.

X-Wing is a CFRG draft construction, not a FIPS standard, so there is nothing for CMVP to validate it against. The ML-KEM inside it can be and is validated -- that is the ml-kem row's cell, not this one.
SM2 is not a NIST-approved curve, so the group cannot sit inside a FIPS 140-3 approved boundary whatever the ML-KEM half does.

why.pure-kex: A device exposes the ML-KEM mechanism and the TLS stack builds the group from it, so the ml-kem row carries this question.
why.hybrid-kex: These rows are named TLS groups, negotiated in a handshake. PKCS#11 exposes mechanisms, and a group is a construction over one -- a device offers the ML-KEM mechanism and the TLS stack builds the group from it, so the KEM row carries this question.
why.composite: PKCS#11 defines no composite-signature mechanism. A caller assembles a composite from its component signatures, each of which is its own mechanism call, so the signature rows carry it.

why.pure-kex: A key exchange group does not sign, and this column is about the signature on a firmware image.
why.kem: A key encapsulation mechanism does not sign, and this column is about the signature on a firmware image. Encrypting firmware is a different question and not one this register asks.
why.hybrid-kex: As for the KEM rows, and doubly so: a negotiated TLS group has no role in signing an image that is verified offline by a bootloader.

questions.title: Which components can sign with pure ML-DSA today?
questions.blurb: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) through the component's own API, in a general release, without a build flag or preview channel. Pure rather than composite: this asks about ML-DSA on its own, not paired with a classical algorithm in one signature. The bar is `available`, so a component that ships it but does not select it by default still counts -- the question is whether you can use it, not whether you get it without asking.

questions.title: Which components can negotiate a hybrid post-quantum TLS group?
questions.blurb: Any one of the IANA-registered hybrid key exchange groups -- X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 or SecP384r1MLKEM1024 -- usable in a TLS 1.3 handshake in a general release. Hybrid rather than pure ML-KEM because hybrid is what browsers and CDNs actually deploy: the classical half means a flaw in the lattice half is not fatal. The bar is `available`, so a group you must configure counts here; the stricter question is the next one.

questions.title: Which components offer a hybrid post-quantum TLS group with no configuration?
questions.blurb: The same three groups as the previous question, but at the bar that matters for traffic actually on the wire: `default`, meaning the group is in the supported-groups list as shipped. This is the question behind "is my fleet already protected against harvest now, decrypt later?", because a group nobody enables protects nobody.

questions.title: Which components can negotiate a pure ML-KEM TLS group?
questions.blurb: Any one of the pure ML-KEM key exchange groups -- MLKEM512, MLKEM768 or MLKEM1024, from draft-ietf-tls-mlkem -- usable in a TLS 1.3 handshake in a general release. Pure rather than hybrid: the whole key exchange rests on ML-KEM, with no classical half. That is what a pure-post-quantum mandate asks for, and it is also why IANA lists all three as Recommended N where X25519MLKEM768 is Y. The bar is `available`; a preview channel or build flag does not count. Added 2026-10-08, when the draft was in the RFC Editor queue.

questions.title: Which components can handle ML-DSA X.509 certificates?
questions.blurb: ML-DSA in certificates and keys -- generating, parsing, signing, verifying or chain-building -- in a general release. The bar is `available`. This is the question that decides whether a post-quantum PKI is deployable at all, and it is deliberately separate from the TLS questions: a stack can negotiate a hybrid key exchange while being unable to validate a post-quantum certificate, and most can.

questions.title: Which components have ML-KEM inside a FIPS 140-3 validated module?
questions.blurb: ML-KEM named in the approved-algorithm list of a module with an ISSUED CMVP certificate -- not a FIPS build, not a submission in the queue, not a vendor's announcement. The bar is `available`, which on the FIPS scale means inside the validated boundary. Running in an approved mode additionally needs the validated version on a tested operating environment, which no register can tell you; this question answers only whether the algorithm is inside the boundary at all.

cells.note: THE FINDING OF THE HARDWARE PASS, and it is a distinction rather than a contradiction. PATROL 2026-10-15: the sentence below that nothing is pending is no longer true -- three AWS KMS HSM submissions are in the CMVP queue (see the evidence); the cell stays `none` because no issued certificate names ML-DSA and the queue names no algorithms, and whether a pending submission should turn a `none` into a gap is for the user. The rest of this note is the 2026-09-13 reading, kept as written. The AWS KMS developer guide says: "AWS KMS creates and protects all ML-DSA keys and signature operations in FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3 validated hardware security modules." That is true. The 2026-09-13 CMVP scan then read the certificate those modules hold -- AWS Key Management Service HSM, certificate 4884, issued 2024-11-18 -- and its approved-algorithm list has thirty entries, not one of them post-quantum. Both facts stand together: the MODULE is validated, and ML-DSA is not a validated ALGORITHM within it, so using it means using a non-approved algorithm inside a validated boundary. Nothing is pending either: no AWS KMS HSM appears on the Modules In Process list, which is why this is `none` and not a gap. This is the same class of claim as the aws-lc-rs one resolved on 2026-09-13 -- a FIPS build is not a FIPS validation -- wearing different clothes: a validated module is not a validated algorithm. Expect the phrasing again; check the approved list every time.

evidence.note: Rewritten 2026-09-29 per the guide's document history ("to accurately list the cryptographic algorithms that AWS KMS supports"). The asymmetric table's only post-quantum row is ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 with key specs ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65, ML_DSA_87; key agreement is ECDH and SM2 only. Still no ML-KEM key spec.

Forward lookup 2026-10-18, two passes: the guide's document-history RSS (readable, unlike the doc-history.html page) has nothing after the 2026-09-29 supported-algorithms rewrite, and the key spec reference re-read today still ends with ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87 ("AWS KMS supports the ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 signing algorithm for all of the ML-DSA key specs"); deriving shared secrets is still ECDH only. No ML-KEM key spec.

cells.note: SETTLED BY AN ENUMERATION, which is what the gap asked for. The Key spec reference lists every key spec a KMS key can have -- SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT, the RSA specs, the elliptic curve specs, the HMAC specs, SM2, and ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87 -- and there is no ML-KEM spec among them. AWS KMS will not create or hold an ML-KEM key. THE CONFUSION THIS RESOLVES IS WORTH KEEPING: AWS does support ML-KEM for KMS, but for the TRANSPORT -- hybrid post-quantum TLS to the KMS endpoints, on non-FIPS endpoints across the aws partition. A reader who sees 'AWS KMS supports ML-KEM' in an announcement is being told about the connection to the service, not about a key the service will hold. The two are one word apart and a migration plan away.

gaps.why: Searched twice with no statement either way. AWS KMS is reached through its own API, SDKs and CLI; PKCS#11 is what AWS offers for CloudHSM, a different service. So the answer is almost certainly that there is no PKCS#11 route to a KMS key, and AWS never says so -- the absence is inferable from the shape of the service and is not stated anywhere read. The register does not promote its own inference to a citation, so this ends as unpublished rather than as a `none`. A third-party PKCS#11 provider for KMS exists, which would be that software's answer and not this component's.

The chain, end to end: aws-lc-rs's FIPS build pulls aws-lc-fips-sys, whose own README says it binds AWS-LC-FIPS 3.0.x (branch fips-2024-09-27); AWS's FIPS.md attributes certificates 5298 (dynamic) and 5314 (static) to that module line; and the security policy for 5314 -- read in full -- does not contain the string ML-DSA anywhere, not even among the non-approved algorithms, while ML-KEM appears 101 times. cells.note: PATROL 2026-09-26: 'currently' ran out. Security World 13.9.3 (2025-12-12) brought ML-KEM to PKCS#11 (firmware 13.8.3+, PostQuantum feature). The history below is kept because it is why the column exists. A CITED `none`, and the sharpest justification for this column in the register. The device implements ML-KEM -- the primitive cell above says so on the same vendor's word -- and an application cannot reach it through PKCS#11 at all, only through Entrust's proprietary nCore API. A register with only a `primitive` column would show this device as ML-KEM-capable and leave the reader to discover the interface gap after buying it. "Currently" is the vendor's word and this cell should be rechecked when Security World moves.

The security policy for certificate 5329 lists the start-up integrity tests: "The bootloader integrity is verified using RSA with 4096 bit key and SHA2-256, using NSBIK public key. The firmware integrity is verified using RSA with 4096 bit key and SHA2-256 using NFIK public key." Both halves of the chain are RSA. THE PATTERN ACROSS THIS CATEGORY, now evidenced rather than suspected: the hardware security modules that hold FIPS-validated post-quantum algorithms FOR CUSTOMERS still sign their OWN firmware classically. Thales Luna T7 uses RSA-4096, Entrust nShield 5s uses RSA-4096, Utimaco uses ECDSA. Crypto4A is the exception and dual-signs with HSS. This is exactly what the firmware column was added to expose: a module whose customer keys are post-quantum and whose root of trust is RSA has moved the problem rather than solved it, and the firmware signing key is the longest-lived key in the device.

evidence.note: The option pack's own release notes (v1.2.1, revision 1.1 of 2025-02-19): "nShield PQC Option Pack v1.2 extends the support for Leighton-Micali hash based signatures (LMS RFC 8554) with three important features: Sectorization, Chunked Merkle Tree Generation, Merkle Tree Caching", on CodeSafe (an NVRAM delegation certificate for the SEE machine is required). LMS only; HSS, XMSS, ML-DSA and ML-KEM are not mentioned. Security World 13.9.6 (2026-07-29) still names no LMS in firmware, so `experimental` stands.

cells.note: THE GAP ASKED WHICH OF TWO CLAIMS APPLIED, and the answer is both, to different products. The Security World 13.9 release notes enumerate the post-quantum algorithms the FIRMWARE gained -- ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA and Pre-Hash ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) -- and LMS is not among them; the words LMS and Leighton do not appear in 50,000 characters of notes. What does offer LMS is the separate Post-Quantum Option Pack, which Entrust describes as enabling "NIST approved code-signing with the Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS)" inside the CodeSafe execution environment. That is exactly what this scale calls `experimental`: a separate add-on the project itself ships, rather than something the shipping firmware does.

THIS FUNCTIONALITY IS CURRENTLY ONLY AVAILABLE VIA nCore."
